articles.text: Piedmont High and Millennium High students attending this year’s Senior Prom took a trip back in time 100 years to the Roaring 20s. The extravagant dance, organized by Piedmont parents was held Saturday, April 29, at The Speakeasy in the Palace Hotel in San Francisco. Students arrived at the high school at 5:30 p.m. wearing 20s attire, paperboy caps, and formal wear before being transported by bus to the dance. Students entered through the speakeasy’s street alias, “Joe’s Clock Shop,” and were welcomed by a pasta and lasagna buffet dinner catered by Tony’s, a restaurant nearby in North Beach. While enjoying dinner, students were entertained by magicians, comics and a dancer performing on an aerial hoop. Mocktails (non-alcoholic drinks) were served at the various bars, students gambled with play money with their friends in the casino room, and danced the night away on a sunken dance floor. Actors portraying flapper dancers lined every corner, leading students through the mysterious history of the speakeasy. Students took advantage of the prop boxes, overflowing with pocket watches, rings and shawls, to pose with in the photo booth. The Speakeasy truly emulated the 20s atmosphere. English teacher, Eduardo Wolbert, helped chaperone the event and enjoyed getting to explore the exciting venue with his students. “The venue was amazing. It had so many rooms and I thought that having the actors all around was really interesting,” said Prom goers dance the night away at The Speakeasy in San Francisco. Photos by Jane Volich

articles.text: Editor: I am a regular pickleball player and a Piedmont resident. I was disappointed to hear that support for permanent courts is waning as a result of some residents near Beach complaining about noise. My husband and I live on Jerome Ave. by Witter Field. We hear the noise of baseball, football, track, etc. on a daily basis. We also hear the sound of pickleball from the middle school, and experience it as much less invasive than the fan cheering, rock and roll music and the PA system from the school. Although there are times when I wish it were quieter (and that the city had kept their promise of no organized play on Sundays), we bought our house near the school and consider athletic play a critical part of a healthy life. If you start trying to make decisions based on sound, you are opening a can of worms. The people who live near Beach, like us, bought their homes knowing there was a school and outdoor activities there. Pickleball may have its own sounds, but they are no more than other sports, and they don’t include loud music and raucous fan cheering. I beseech you to resolve this conflict in favor of permanent courts. The pickleball community is a huge asset to the city but won’t continue to be willing to put up with temporary courts that are inadequate in so many ways. –Paula Flamm Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at Mulberry’s Market, and Piedmont Shell at Grand & Wildwood Ave. Copies of the paper may be purchased for $1 at all locations during business hours. While in jail Dr. King read a full page advertisement in a local paper signed by eight prominent white clergyman (Protestant, Catholic and Jewish) decrying his presence in their city and labeling him an unwanted, unnecessary and inflammatory outsider. This letter hurt and distressed him. Over the period of his incarceration, he wrote his response in the margins of the paper and on whatever scraps of paper he could find and gave what he wrote to his attorney, Clarence B. Jones, to smuggle out. Jones delivered what King had written to King’s chief of staff, Wyatt Tee Walker, who, along with King’s personal secretary, Dora McDonald, put together the manuscript that was first published shortly thereafter by a Quaker publication. It was later published on June 12, 1963 by a national religious publication, The Christian Century, where King was a contributing editor. articles.text: Work at the Piedmont Community Pool site is continuing on schedule, with contractors now building a retaining wall for the new pool. Since April 21 the contractors from Wickman Development & Construction have been drilling concrete piers for the wall with a large auger and placing steel cages in the holes for reinforcement. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the contractors currently have completed about 385 feet of retaining wall along Bonita Avenue near the tennis courts, with “interior, site retaining walls that will be constructed later.” The process of drilling piers for the wall is expected to last through mid-May, after which the contractors will start to bring steel and concrete on-site, while off-hauling soil off-site. “By mid-May, there will be more trucking activity,” Gonzales said. “The off-haul won’t be every day, but it’ll be about an eight-week period, going through June. The grading and retaining wall work overall should take up at least the next two months, also through June.” As construction continues, the GEOCON Consultants will perform geotechnical testing for the retaining wall. Through this process, engineers which specialize in soil will make design recommendations as to how the wall can be constructed on existing soil types at the site. Gonzales said that GEOCON consultants will also inspect materials involved in the retaining wall construction, “making sure that the steel used is strong enough and welded correctly, also testing concrete samples to make sure that it’s the right strength.” He added that the company was “one of the first to start on this [pool project] on-site; they took soil samples to look at existing site conditions two years ago, in 2021.” Griffin Structures, the project manager, will oversee work performed by GEOCON. Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions or comments about the pool project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. A retaining wall is currently under construction at the Community Pool site.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is soliciting suggestions from community members willing to serve on a task force that would help develop a plan for how to electrify Piedmont’s residences. The Building Electrification Strategy Task Force, to be appointed by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, will work with staff to better understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a strategic framework for equitably moving Piedmont’s building stock off of natural gas. Letters of interest due May 16 The city staff has approached several community members who have previously engaged with the City on electrification and sustainability initiatives about their potential interest in serving on the task force. To ensure that the task force incorporates diverse perspectives and wide-ranging expertise, we are also soliciting interest from the community at large. If you think you can help, send an email to ElectrificationTaskForce@piedmont.ca.gov by Tuesday, May 16 describing why you’re interested in serving on the task force, and what skills, experience, or perspective you would bring. Residential electrification Transitioning Piedmont’s existing residences from natural gas to clean electricity is crucial for meeting the city’s emission reduction targets established in the City’s Climate Action Plan. Despite substantial investment in climate action work – which has earned a Beacon Spotlight Award for Sustainability Best Practices from the Institute for Local Government for two consecutive years – Piedmont is not presently on track to meet its greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals. The gap is largely due to natural gas use in residential buildings, which accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, heating and cooling these homes requires greater than average energy use. For each year between 2017 and 2020, annual emissions just from residential buildings exceeded Climate Action Plan targets for total emissions in Piedmont by 2050. Most of these emissions came from natural gas furnaces and water heaters. The City is now seeking to draw on the wealth of expertise within our community to create a strategic plan for expediting this transition. The Task Force will be charged with developing an Existing Building Electrification Strategy that will guide future policies and programs related to residential building electrification. For questions about letters of interest or the Electrification Task Force, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at jtulloch@piedmont. ca.gov or 420-3041. “We can’t beat ‘em, and they won’t let us join ‘em.”

articles.text: The city is implementing additional safety measures around the community pool construction site due to increased truck traffic in the coming weeks. Starting next Monday, May 8: • The construction fence on Magnolia Avenue will be extended farther into the street, creating a separate travel lane for trucks inside the fence • The lane will remain open to cars for through-travel • The school pick-up and dropoff area will remain in place These measures will separate trucks from pedestrian activity on Magnolia Avenue. The increased truck traffic is due to excavation and soil removal activity at the pool construction site, and is expected to last eight weeks, through early June. Trucks will enter the construction site at Hillside and Magnolia, be loaded inside the site, then exit directly onto Bonita Avenue. To minimize traffic disruption, truck activity will take place outside of school drop-off and pick-up periods (8-9 a.m., 2-3:30 p.m.). For questions about the traffic changes on Magnolia Avenue, contact Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. articles.text: The Mended Hearts, Inc. (MHI) is the largest cardiovascular support organization in the world and a national and community-based non-profit organization. It has been offering the gift of hope to heart disease patients, their families and caregivers. and will host a Zoom seminar this Saturday, May 6, at 10:00 a.m. Saturday’s program will include Mended Hearts and the American Society for Preventive Cardiology for Part 1 of Mended Hearts’ Risk Reduction Webinar Series. In this session they look at controlling your cholesterol and modifying your diet to reduce your risk of heart disease, and associated diseases. Cholesterol has a central role in atherosclerosis, which is the build-up of cholesterol in our arteries. Treating this build up is central to lowering heart disease. There are several methods of LDL Cholesterol reduction, including statins, Ezetimibe, and the PCSK-9 inhibitors. In this first of six Risk Reduction webinars, they review the message that dieting for weight loss is NOT the same as dieting for your heart’s health. As we learned in last month’s webinar on the Connection Between Alzheimer’s Disease and the Heart, several recent studies show that your diet and exercise are factors under your control that also reduce your risk of Alzheimer’s Disease. Founded by Dr. Dwight E. Harken, MHI was started with four of Dr. Harken’s open heart surgery patients. In January 1951 Dr. Harken asked one of the first 50 patients to ever have heart surgery, and three other post-surgery heart patients to meet at the hospital. They spoke of their new feeling of well-being, their plans and hopes for the future — and with renewed happiness they spoke of their “mended hearts.” They realized how wonderful it would be to provide support and help others facing the same experience. In the 70 years since then, Mended Hearts has expanded to provide support and education across the country and around the world. Today there are over 100,000 members, 260 chapters and 350 participating hospitals in the US. The local Oakland chapter has been in existence for over 30 years. In addition to visiting patients at Oakland’s Summit Hospital, the chapter has monthly meetings focused on education related to heart health. articles.text: Diversity Day, one of Piedmont Middle School’s most popular events, returned on Monday, April 24 after a three-year absence due to the COVID pandemic. Yearbook teacher Anne Smith, who has helped organize it for many years, revived the event which brings speakers to the school to share their various stories and demonstrate their talents. It encompasses a wide breadth of topics relevant to ethnic, social and cultural diversity. The morning started off with two groups of assemblies in the MPR, with the middle school Jazz Band performing. 6th grader Francesca Clark, a member of the school’s Green Team, and 8th grader Zoe Snyder each gave a Land Acknowledgement. In their classes, before attending speaker workshops, teachers familiarized their students with the speakers’ biographies. “What is Diversity?” classes brainstormed and came up with responses including: ethnicity, gender, personality, religion, age, likes and dislikes, learning styles, and physical traits. Each class attended two of the Lance McGee a.k.a. “Unique Derique” demonstrates “Hambone” body percussion and tells of its origins from times of slavery. 6th grade teacher Hillary Voigt (left) playing Goal Ball blindfolded in the Buzz Redford gym. Mina Herrgott (left) with Raquel Jetè in Jetè’s demonstration on “Headwraps: A Black Woman’s History.” PMS 6th grade teacher Lea Lotia invited her father, Aquil Lotia, to talk to students on Diversity Fay about his experience growing up in Pakistan. Michael Bracamonte’s 6th grade Core students Jordan Morris-Price (left), Gael Fierro, Emily Hu, Sharlize Sahagon, and Kayleigh Anderson hang up Wish and Action Tags. 14 different workshops offered. Some of the speakers included: • Eliezer Cohn: “History of Anti-Semitism” • Grace Patterson and Morgan Lewis: “Representation and Equity in Film” • Bri Blue: “Spoken Word Artist” • Ali Cannon and Thomas Kennard: “Transgender Journeys: Stories of Becoming Men” • Raquel Jetè: “Headwraps: A Black Woman’s History” • Oluyemi and Ijeoma Thomas: “Jazz Music Workshop” • Unique Derique McGee: “Hambone Body Percussion” Unique Derique (Lance McGee), gave a powerful demonstration to 8th graders about the origins and importance of Hambone body percussion. McGee explained how using the body as a percussive instrument surfaced in the times of slavery after the Djembe Drum was taken away from slaves. articles.text: There is a wonderful artist, Amber Share, who takes the onestar ratings of National Parks and turns them into beautiful, handdrawn and lettered postcards. Yosemite features the caption, “Trees block the view and there are too many gray rocks.” Joshua Tree is, “The only thing to do here is walk around the desert.” And a personal favorite, Pinnacles: “A bunch of rocks. Big deal.” Alarmingly, these reviews were written by adults, but they strike a stark resemblance to the complaints of a child who’s been dragged on a walk. “This is boring.” “There’s nothing to do.” “My feet hurt.” Not everyone has an inherent appreciation of the outdoors and if the family nature hikes feel like an uphill battle, here is some reassurance that you are doing the right thing, Time outside is good for us. The simple act of getting outside reduces stress, regulates emotions, and improves overall health. While most adults enjoy a hearty trail walk, many children are so used to being entertained that nature, by just existing, is boring. To get children outside and with joy the framing and set-up matters. Nature needs to be more than something to play in, but something to play with. Assuming there is groundwork Building appreciation for nature through play for safety and no destruction to protected spaces, playing with nature might look like the following: • Throwing rocks into a creek • Digging a hole in the sand • Climbing on top of a fallen tree or large rock • Picking up a HUGE stick • Picking up another HUGE stick and starting to build a fort While these activities may cause a knee-jerk “stop that!”, they all build a level of freedom and exploration that puts nature at the center of a child’s adventure. Unlike a video game or TV show with a predetermined plot, children are foraging a path on their own when they play outside. Their brains are seeing possibility in a rock and using creativity to overcome the challenges of getting up high or making a fort. The benefits of being in nature don’t change if you’re climbing a tree or taking a walk - all that matters is getting out there. articles.text: Smolko places 2nd in singles, Breber 4th Piedmont brought seven players to this year’s WACC Tournament: Will Tenney (left), Arun Brahma, Nick King, Ben Breber, Lucas Smolko, Nate Welch, and Ethan Pham. After finishing the regular season in 2nd place, Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team competed in the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference on Friday and Saturday, April 28-29 at Chabot College in Hayward. Freshman Lucas Smolko reached the finals in the singles bracket, junior Carson Breber reached the semifinals in singles, and Arun Brahma and Nate Welch placed fifth in the doubles bracket. Smolko earned the No. 2 seed and a first-round bye. He defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Lucas Tanaka 6-1, 6-1 in the second-round and followed up with a 6-1, 6-1 victory over Colin Sweeney of O’Dowd to close the first day of action. In the semifinals on Saturday, Smolko defeated Berkeley’s Leighton Sproul in three sets, 6-2, 2-6, 6-4. “It was an interesting match for me because I’ve practiced against Leighton a lot. We’ve almost always had close matches and I knew it could go either way. There were a lot of emotions running through my mind. In the first set, I was a bit more aggressive, then I started to get a bit tentative in the second,” said Smolko following the semifinals. Advancing to the finals, he faced top-seeded Elijah Cho of San Leandro, and took the Pirates’ senior to three sets before falling in a heated final, 7-5, 2-6, 7-5. In the first set, Smolko rallied from being down 4-1 to tie the match set at 5-5. Cho won the next two games to claim victory in the first set. Smolko played a strong second set, winning his fifth point as the returner with a winning forehand, and then won the final game as the server. The third set was nearly identical to the first. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team pushed favored Bishop O’Dowd to the limit before falling 11-9 in the league championship game ay O’Dowd on Friday, April 28. In a double header between both schools. Piedmont’s boys team beat the Dragons 14-6 for its 6th consecutive league championship. O’Dowd jumped out to a 5-1 lead, but the Highlanders rallied to tie the game at 7-7 in the early minutes of the second half. However, BOD scored three consecutive goals in a span of two minutes to give the Dragons the edge. It was a strong performance from Piedmont after losing to Bishop O’Dowd 14-7 on March 17. “It was a tough game. We had to climb a mountain. I’m super proud of the girls to keep their heads in the game and then tie it 7-7,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. “The last time we played them, we walked out of the first half down 2-8. This time we had a plan. It ended up being a few possessions’ difference at the end of the game.” Molly Ashton scored two goals and had one assist against O’Dowd. Ruby Guzdar had four goals and an assist versus the Dragons. Staff Photos Coach Carlton Chan with Piedmont lacrosse players during their narrow 11-9 loss to Bishop O’Dowd in the league championship game. “We had it… we had it,” said Chan, shaking his head. “It’s rough. Last year was the first year we lost to them after having a six-year streak against them,” explained senior leader Molly Ashton. “We came out strong like we were already in mid-game form. We’ve had trouble with that, but this time we came out really fast, and I don’t think they were expecting that,” mentioned Ashton. Piedmont has received a No. 13 seed in the post-season North Coast Section playoffs, and faced No. 4 San Marin last night, Tuesday, May 2. results. Match recap O’Dowd jumped out to an early 2-0 lead before freshman Peyton Watson scored six minutes into the first half. But O’Dowd tacked on three goals for a comfortable 5-1 lead with 16:25 left in the half. Ruby Guzdar scored on a feed from Ashton with 9:36 left to narrow the score to 5-3. O’Dowd’s Lucy Yu, the daughter of Piedmont boys’ lacrosse coach Al Yu, scored following a shooting space penalty, and BOD’s Mariah Branscomb netted her third goal of the match to make it 7-3 with 7:59 left in the first half. However, Guzdar scored with a wraparound goal with 5:39 to play, followed Watson recovering a ground ball in front of O’Dowd’s net to score with 3:44 to play. With 1:01 left, Guzdar found Ashton for a goal to bring PHS within one goal, down 7-6. In the second half, the teams traded possession back and forth through the opening 10 minutes until Guzdar scored with 15:20 left, tying the game for the first time at 7-7. However, Yu scored on another shooting space opportunity. But Piedmont’s Chloe Graham then scored to tie the match at 8-8 with 13:14 remaining. O’Dowd then went on a scoring run with a shooting space goal, a wraparound goal by Yu, and another shooting space conversion to make it 11-8. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team got its North Coast Section journey started with a 3-0 win against Encinal and advancing to the second round of the playoffs. Playing on Tuesday, May 2 as the No. 6 seed (last year it was seeded No. 11), the Highlanders defeated No. 11 Encinal 3-0 by scores of 25-15, 25-19, 25-22 in a game played in the middle school gym due to testing occupying Piedmont’s high school gym. “I’m excited. We worked really hard the past couple of days. We’ve never played in this gym. We played Encinal before but they were able to beat us last time we played them. We had a game plan and brought great energy,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It is the team’s second consecutive season to win a game in NCS after upsetting No. 6 Analy last year. “We came in a lot stronger this year. Last year was my first year being the head coach. This year, I knew what we were capable of. We have seven great seniors and I’ve been with them since they were sophomores,” said Cardenas. “It’s feeling amazing. Year 2 in NCS. It’s been a massive journey. Some of us were on the B-team back in middle school and we were always the underdogs. Now, we almost doubled our wins total from last season. We have a really special group,” said senior leader Wilson Wong. It was a productive opening round for freshman Albert Bellingrath, who recorded two kills and three consecutive aces in the second game and made a difference as middle blocker. “Seeing him walk into tryouts was a big confidence booster because we all saw the potential in him,” said Wong. Having a freshman be the tallest player on the team got everyone hyped.” Match recap Piedmont won the first game 25-15 with John Champion slamming down a spike for the winning point. In the second game, Encinal opened with a 3-1 lead but Piedmont went on to score six unanswered points to lead 7-3. The Jets eventually took the lead at 13-12, but Piedmont regained their advantage at 15-14. Encinal tied the match at 15-15 and 18-18 but never went ahead. From there, PHS scored seven of the last eight points, including a spike by Eric Olaru-Hagen, three straight aces by Bellingrath, and a kill by Champion. Encinal got out to a 5-1 lead to start the third game, but Piedmont scored eight of the next 11 points and regain the lead at 8-7. The Jets eventually got back to the front at 19-18 until Piedmont tied the match at 22-22. An interesting turning point awarded PHS’ 22nd point when coach Cardenas challenged a ruling when Encinal’s back row player illegal hit a ball. PHS went ahead 23-22 on an offensive error by Encinal, then Owen Kelly scored on a sneaky push to an open area on the floor. With match point, Brayden Ellis sent a looping serve to the middle of the Jets court, landing for the match-winner. Final stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-6 overall) will face the winner of No. 3 Acalanes and No. 14 Marin Catholic on Thursday, May 4. Freshman Albert Bellingrath had a productive game against Encinal, recording three consecutive aces in the third set.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ relay teams won league titles and finished their season undefeated. Pictured are coach Colby Price (left), Abigail Jacoby, Josie Oesterer, Taylor Rolefson, Sonja ten Grotenhuis and Sydney Olson. The Piedmont High swim team – the team with no hometown pool – traveled to Chabot College in Hayward for the Western Alameda County Conference Championship on Friday, April 28. The girls’ team won three events on the day. Piedmont’s girls’ 200 Medley Relay and 400 Freestyle Relay team completed an undefeated season and continued by winning three events at the league championship. Their 200 medley includes junior Josie Oesterer on the backstroke, freshman Abigail Jacoby on the breaststroke, junior Taylor Rolefson on butterfly and sophomore Sonja ten Grotenhuis as the final leg for the freestyle, defeating eight teams with a time of 1:54.74. “It was crazy. I knew I got out to a lead when I was in the pool. When I finished my leg all my teammates behind the block were going crazy,” said ten Grotenhuis. The race came down to the wire with Piedmont defeating Berkeley by .71 of a second. Oesterer finished her leg of the race with a time of 30.50, followed by Jacoby clocking a 31.98. articles.text: Museum visitors view an item in MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition. San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with the exhibit Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibit is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. General Dentistry & Advanced Prosthodontics
articles.title: MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition on view through August 20

articles.text: Artwork by John Singer Sargent is currently on view at the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park through May 14. Sargent (1856 -1925) is regarded as the premiere portraitist of his era and is also known for his paintings of churches, coastlines, gardens and royal venues. This exhibition highlights his love of Spanish culture and the time he spent in Spain. The exhibit includes Sargent’s oils, watercolors, and drawings, as well as never-before-exhibited photographs showcasing the Mediterranean people, architecture, and urban and rural landscapes. The exhibit is displayed in the museum’s Rosekrans Court. For tickets and for more information, visit https://www.famsf. org. John Singer Sargent (American, 1856–1925). La Carmencita, 1890. articles.text: Play ends this Sunday, May 7 American Conservatory Theatre’s newest play Poor Yella Rednecks: Vietgone 2 is being performed through May 7. Written by Qui Nguyen, it is a sequel to the popular Vietgone which premiered at the Strand Theater five years ago. Poor Yella Rednecks is part two in a trilogy by Nguyen. The story follows a Vietnamese family who left war-torn Saigon for rural Arkansas in the 1970’s. Married couple Tong and Quang encounter challenges in their new home: namely, their low-wage jobs don’t afford many luxuries, and their son is struggling to keep up with his peers as he tries to learn a new language. “This story goes deep while soaring high,” said ACT Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “It’s a personal exploration of the American Dream specific to a Vietnamese immigrant family and first-gen American experience, full of compromise, joy, hardscrabble setback, and love.” “I’m thrilled to be back in San Francisco at one of my favorite theaters in the country. This sequel to Vietgone promises to be just as exciting. Qui’s words will make you want to laugh and dance at the same time,” said director Jaime Castañeda. Cast members inlude Will Dao, Christine Jamlig, Hyunmin Rhee, Jomar Tagatac and Jenny Nguyen Nelson. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ poor-yella-rednecks-vietgone-2/. articles.text: Steven Spielberg’s The Fablemans, a semi-autobiographical, coming-of-age story, was nominated for seven Oscars, including Best Picture, at this year’s 2023 Academy Awards. Consider it a memoir of sorts that attempts to share with the audience how this extraordinarily talented and prolific filmmaker came to love cinema as a form of storytelling. Regarding the title, I wondered if Spielberg chose the family’s last name “Fableman,” as a way of signaling to the audience that he has devoted his life to entertaining audiences worldwide using the medium of film. Collaborating with screenwriter and Pulitzer Prize award-winning playwright Tony Kushner of Berkeley Rep fame, they create a series of vignettes focusing on the early years of one Sammy Fableman (later the 16-year-old Gabriel LaBelle). The movie opens with young Sammy (Mateo Zoryan Francis DeFord) going with his parents, Mitzi and Burt (Michelle Williams and Paul Dano), to see The Greatest Show on Earth, a larger than life, circus-themed tale released by Cecil B. DeMille in 1952. Wideeyed, Sammy watches a spectacular, jaw-dropping train crash that completely enthralls him and proves unforgettable. How was that done, he wonders? And could he recreate that eye-popping moment? And thus began Sammy’s love affair with cameras, celluloid, and those magical images that can be captured on what was then known as “the silver screen.” As well, Spielberg shares with the audience his anxiety about his parents (who eventually split up), encounters blatant anti-Semitism in high school, and recruits his family (parents and sisters) and peers to make what are in essence grainy, rough-cut home movies. He also includes his first adolescent romance with an enthusiastic girl who is devoted to Jesus (her room is covered with Christ’s image), yet is fascinated by the fact that Sammy is Jewish. While his dad’s work takes the family west, from New Jersey to Arizona to California, Sammy’s camera is always close by. And it’s while learning to edit his films, he comes to realize that not only can movies entertain, but they can reveal. And it’s while editing and splicing recently shot footage that he inadvertently discovers, to his chagrin, that his mother is enamored with Burt’s best friend “Uncle” Benny (Seth Rogen), who is all but a member of the family. While I have always been part of that cohort referred to as Spielberg’s fandom, beginning with Jaws, and the countless films that followed such as E.T., Indiana Jones, Empire of the Sun, Always, etc, I found The Fablemans a bit flat and restrained. Something is missing, perhaps a certain “let er rip” energy that has always defined Spielberg’s work. It’s as if The Fablemans is a home movie and we are guests in his living room. Why it was nominated for seven Oscars is a puzzle. The Fablemans. Written and directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Michelle Williams, Paul Dano, Seth Rogen. 2 hrs., 31 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: In I’ll See You in My Dreams, writer and director Bret Haley gets just right the essence of Carol, a 72-year-old retired school teacher and widow, played with charming insight by Blythe Danner. To Haley’s credit, he avoids clichés such as “senior citizen” or “the golden years.” And no one is cranky or a hard case curmudgeon. In every respect, Dreams is a sweet and touching film about discovering that life can still be unexpectedly renewed and on occasion a surprise. Carol lost her husband some 20 years ago in a plane crash and has lived an orderly, if somewhat insular life ever since. She takes genuine pleasure in her L.A. home with a pool and garden and never feels weighted by the solitude that frames each day. She wakes at exactly six, makes coffee, and plans her day: time in the garden, a salad for lunch, perhaps a game of cards with her three friends (Rhea Pearlman, Mary Kay Place and June Squibb), all residents of a nearby active retirement community. Her only daily companion is Hazel, a much loved and aging dog. Above all, this is a subtle character study of a lovely if cautious woman surrounded by a quiet routine that, after all these years, she now welcomes. The opening set up finds her waking in the early hours of the morning, realizing that Hazel is not sleeping on the bed. Concerned, she searches the house. Smash cut to the vet hospital where Hazel is close to death. In a moving and heartfelt scene, Carol leans over the stainless steel table and places her hand on Hazel’s forehead as her cherished dog slowly slips away. Hazel’s death pushes Carol out of her comfort zone, and as a result things begin to happen in her life. She befriends Lloyd, the pool guy, a young man who describes how he feels decidedly unmoored. She meets Bill (Sam Elliot), long ago divorced, and also a resident of the retirement community. Their mutual fondness for one another, which evolves in small increments, ultimately leads to a brief romantic interlude that clearly surprises Carol. In a nice way. As it does Bill. If there is a sense of sadness to Dreams – more like a mild melancholy – it resides with the growing realization, voiced by Carol to her daughter, Kat (Malin Ackerman), that life is increasingly finite and far closer to its conclusion that not. The years ahead grow fewer. Behind her are countless incandescent images, memories of her past to be savored and perhaps wept over. She understands that in youth our years are spent like so much loose change, unthinking. Until we don’t, finally understanding that time is all we have and how we spend it comprises the sum total of our lives. Carol and her friends know this and you can almost hear them say, “Carpe diem!” as they plan in the final scene a grand and glorious adventure, just the four of them. So many of our movies are youth-driven. Romantic comedies can seem manic, frenetic, as young people search for what is missing in their lives. Someone else. Something else. Both. Often with abandon and excess. What marks Dreams is its grace, its carefully crafted and beautifully written sensitivity. It’s a film to be savored and enjoyed and contemplated. Between the lines and scenes there is wisdom and intelligence without even one patronizing, overly sentimentalized moment. It’s gently honest and replete with wonderful performances. I’ll See You in My Dreams. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Blythe Danner, Sam Elliot, Malin Akerman. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on WUDU/Prime/HBO MAX/Apple tv.

articles.text: I’m way beyond the demographic that Marvel Comics is aiming for with Spider-Man: Homecoming. However, I think the stable of writers who worked on the script (six in all) missed a great opportunity to make a spot-on film. What the Marvel superhero creators (aka Marvel Cinematic Universe) have done, at least in the case of Spider-Man, is box themselves in with what they assume is the demand for overthe-top CGI action stuff. Here’s the deal: Spider-Man (he’s never been a man) is and always has been a kid. Young Peter Parker (in this incarnation played by Tom Holland) is a superhero, but a kid superhero. And it’s being an adolescent that makes him unique and special. With Homecoming they come close to keeping the story focused on Peter Parker’s high school issues, until they introduce Adrian Toomes, aka the Vulture (Michael Keaton). He’s totally unnecessary. This is a movie that doesn’t need a nasty villain. And it didn’t need an act three-wham!/ bam!/kaboom! event. When you’re 15-years-old and a sophomore in high school you spend most of your time figuring out all the changes you’re going through. And if you’re discovering that on top of dealing with superhero abilities, well, that means you have a full plate. Peter is a nerd, a geek. He’s on the debate team and was a member of the band. He loves chess. He’s smart. Teachers love smart kids who are free of attitude, so naturally he’s ripe to be picked on by the hard-case crowd. But, alas, Homecoming has a pretty bogus plot, one that is totally beside the point. As well, Peter doesn’t need mentoring by Iron Man. What does he know about kids? Homecoming is the sixth film in the Spiderman series and was ready for a new direction. Instead the tween/newbie teen crowd got more of the same. Coulda, shoulda been about Peter going to Queen’s Midtown High School of Science and all that entails, mixed with Spider-Man as your neighborhood crime stopper. That’s it. Full stop. Spider-Man: Homecoming. Directed by Jon Watts. Starring Tom Holland, Michael Keaton and Jacob Batalon. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Apparently Universal Studios has launched a panoply franchise of sorts, the goal being to resurrect those iconic monsters that chilled audiences in the 20s, 30s and well into the 50s. The Mummy is the first of what Universal calls the Dark Universe. If this picture is an example of what lies ahead, I’d judge the yet to be realized franchise is off to a limp start. I confess that I would welcome the chance to see how they update one of my boyhood favorites, The Creature From the Black Lagoon. I will never forget raising goosebumps on top of goosebumps as a group of unsuspecting scientists remains topside in a research boat, floating in an ominous jungle lagoon, while a man/fish, covered in scales with large webbed hands, swims just beneath the surface, waiting. Unfortunately, the recent incarnation of The Mummy is a mess, and the narrative incoherency chronic. No matter that the idea of a resurrected mummy, trailing bandages while staggering after archeologists who never ever should have opened its sarcophagus, dates back to Boris Karloff in the first 1932 version, then brought back in the 1999 Brendan Fraser trilogy, featuring Egyptian tombs and curses and Fraser as a swash-buckling, Indiana Jones type. Same gauzy bandages, indeed, but just a bit more elaborate regarding special effects and artifacts and if memory serves lots of black beetles and sandstorms. Which brings us to 2017 and the durable and protean Tom Cruise who portrays Nick Morton, a mercenary artifact hunter who is also happens to be in the army, and is accompanied by his sidekick Chris Vail (Jake Johnson). The setting is Iraq. A drone missile blows a deep hole in the village square exposing an enormous Egyptian stone mien that curiously happens to be in Mesopotamia. Cue Jenny Halsey (Annabelle Wallis), archeologist, who appears and recognizes that what has been exposed is a tomb or sorts and must immediately be Sofia Boutella as Ahmanet in The Mummy investigated. And so begins a barely intelligible story about an ancient Egyptian princess, Ahmanet (Sofia Boutella), who commits patricide and is wrapped and buried alive in an evil looking sarcophagus filled with mercury (don’t ask). Clearly the hieroglyphics covering the casket make clear that it would be best to not open same. Standard trope. Jenny tries to explain this to Nick, but his eyes glaze over wondering only what such an artifact might bring on the black market. His favorite hieroglyphic is “show me the money,” which is a line we’ve heard before. There is a plane ride that is the best part of the movie – that would be where Nick, Chris and Jenny accompany the sarcophagus back to England and the large military plane goes down, overwhelmed by a flock of crows. It’s quite a gravity-defying ride. The rest of the movie challenges you to suspend your disbelief and try not to say, “as if.” Nick and Jenny are chased, they run, again they chase, and run some more. Who’s chasing them? How about 12th century Crusaders released from their tombs. And there’s a dagger, a missing red stone that Ahmanet really, really wants to get a hold of. If she kills Nick with the dagger, that will release Set, Egyptian god of death. Follow? No? Me neither. There are more crows and rats and even a Dr. Jekyll (Russell Crowe) appears who is taking regular injections to ward off becoming a grim Mr. Hyde. Seriously. Suffice it to say that the sarcophagus is no ark and Cruise is no Indy. When in doubt, add more bandages, unless said mummy is a shapely princess, then less is definitely more. If there is eternal life then it rests with Tom Cruise’s abs which are on display and don’t look 54-years-old. I can’t recall if said abs appeared in the most recent Mission Impossible. Now that’s a franchise that has yet to disappoint. The Mummy. Directed by Alex Kurtzman. Starring Tom Cruise, Russell Crowe, Annabelle Wallis. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: We stumble through life and taxes, and then we meet the compact Smuin Ballet which has emerged from the pandemic seemingly unscathed. Its newest Bay Area run showed off 17 beautifully coordinated and trained dancers in pieces new and old, bursting with precision and energy. Purists may carp about the troupe’s leanings toward the commercial, but this group under Celia Fushille offers both sides, serving up contemporary with a capital C, abetted by the new associate director and adroit choreographer Amy Seiwert. The engrossing opening-night program offered the wake-up call via a twin-barrel blast of culture: Val Caniparoli’s earth-shaking foray into a stormy percussive world, and Seiwert’s light-hearted world premiere to French songs so much in the spirit of founder Michael Smuin. (Smuin in early years had actually performed as a nightclub show duo with partner-spouse Paula Tracy – not exactly your typical dancer’s CV.) Seiwert’s piece “French Kiss” showed itself as airy as a sunny Sunday on the Champs-Élysées, with skirts in alluring sherbet-pastel colors, whirled about by cosmopolitan sophisticates. The dozen players flowed on and off stage as smooth as silk, mostly in pairs. No, no kisses, but a lot of youthful exuberance to French songs from the Pink Martini ensemble. Perhaps with a bow to Magritte, a group of dancers hit the stage flourishing black umbrellas, evolving into part of the whimsical décor. Another Seiwert-only touch was the mannequin pas de deux, so appropriate for these AI days, with life-size plastic figures wheeled around by flesh-andblood partners. This sure-fire crowd-pleaser Photo by Chris Hardy Smuin artists Ricardo Dyer (left), Alison Ramoran, Brennan Wall, Marc LaPierre, and Mengjun Chen with the company in Amy Seiwert’s world premiere of French Kiss, unveiled in Smuin’s “Dance Series 2” touring the Bay Area through May 28. capped the first night at the Lesher Center. And yet what bowled me most over was Caniparoli’s rugged ritual Swipe (2011), as jostling as driving with four flat tires. The bold shoulder swivel-thrusts and bobbing necks had me instinctively flexing muscles dormant for ages. The performers provocatively raised and worked hands on high – I couldn’t tell whether they were waving to Aunt Matilda in the 12th row or simply satirizing empty political speeches, which already anticipate 2024. The high point April 28 was a pairing of Cassidy Isaacson and João Sampaio, nimble and athletic to the core. Among Caniparoli’s quirky enigmas came a woman’s extended leg (Isaacson again) doing a breath-taking full-360 like a sweep-second hand of a clock, in a display of flexibility par excellence, one that’s very rarely done on stage. The program opened with Katarzyna Skarpetowska’s Sextette for four women and two men dancing to Bach, memorable for the skyward leaps of Ricardo Dyer, a dabbler in lofty elevation. In between, Smuin’s duet “Dream” was a vehicle for ballerina Tessa Barbour in a long voluptuous formal, later partnered by the Brazilian flash Sampaio. Of note in this program was the meticulous preparation of the ensemble, with letter-perfect formations, pliable bodies, and ballet moves to remember. Casts change nightly. All the music is prerecorded. Seiwert, just promoted to associate artistic director, turned up at intermission to meet patrons, along with Fushille, in a refreshing turnabout from those troupes that rarely show their directors offstage. SMUIN CONTEMPORARY BALLET opened its 29th season April 28-29 at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center, then San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center May 5-14, and Mountain View’s CPA May 25-28. Details online, www. smuinballet.org. www. something humorous .com

articles.text: If you’ve done any estate planning, or even if you’re just familiar with it, you probably know the basics — that is, a comprehensive estate plan can help you pass on assets to your family while also achieving other goals, such as designating someone to take care of your affairs if you become unable to do so. But you may not know about some other estate-planning issues that could prove important in your life: • Power of attorney for students Children heading off to college may be considered legal adults in many states. Consequently, you, as a parent, may not have any control over medical treatment if your child faces a sudden, serious illness or is involved in an accident. Instead, a doctor who doesn’t know your child or your family may decide on a course of action of which you might not approve. To help prevent this, you may want to have your college student sign a medical power of attorney form, which will allow you to make decisions on your child’s behalf if doctors don’t think your child can make those choices. You might also want to combine the medical power of attorney with an advance health care directive or living will, which lets you specify actions you do or don’t want to happen. In any case, consult with your legal advisor before taking any of these steps. • Community property versus common law Not all states treat married couples’ possessions equally. If you live in a community property state, the property you acquire during your marriage is generally considered to be owned in equal halves by each spouse, with some exceptions. But if you live in a common law state, the property you obtain while you’re married is not automatically owned by both spouses. In these states, if you buy some property, you own it, unless you decide to put it in the name of yourself and your spouse. This doesn’t necessarily mean that your spouse has no rights, because common law states typically have rules that guard surviving spouses from being disinherited. articles.text: A treat awaits in time for Mother’s Day • Is this fudgy pudding cake on your radar? As the cake bakes, a thick, rich sauce forms on the bottom of the pan, leaving a light, brownie-like cake atop. It’s a marvel to watch as it bakes, and always a crowd pleaser. The recipe scores bonus points as an easy-peasy dessert to fill the bill for newer bakers to prepare for Mother’s Day. This recipe likely dates back to the late- ‘70’s from a fine food shop in Philadelphia. Since then, countless recipes have appeared, and I’ve tweaked my own version over the years. This one has less sugar but still retains a very deep, rich chocolate-y indulgence using a handful of few ingredients, many of which you likely have on hand most of the time! Take note: this cake has a unique process. The pudding layer is achieved by adding the ingredients in a very unconventional way. The thick cake batter forms the base, but then you add the “pudding” on top, which consists of brown sugar, more cocoa powder and hot coffee or water. The liquid=y pudding ingredients begin sinking once in the oven, and the resulting cake is atop the fudge-y pudding. It’s chemistry, or magic. You decide. • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted then cooled slightly 3/4 cup chocolate chips For the pudding: • 2/3 cup light brown sugar • 1/4 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 1-1/2 cups brewed coffee or very hot water INSTRUCTIONS Chocolate Pudding Cake Adapted from King Arthur Baking INGREDIENTS For the cake: • 1-1/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 3/4 cup whole milk, room temperature • 1 large egg, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Set a rimmed baking sheet on the rack to catch any drips and/or bake individual ramekins. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Butter an 8ʺ square pan, or eight 8-ounce ramekins. For the cake: In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and cocoa powder. Make sure there are no large clumps of cocoa powder, which you can pinch between your fingers to separate. Stir in the milk, egg, vanilla, and melted butter, mixing until smooth. Chocolate Pudding Cake – magic in the making A treat awaits in time for Mother’s Day By Deborah Quok • Is this fudgy pudding cake on your radar? As the cake bakes, a thick, rich sauce forms on the bottom of the pan, leaving a light, brownie-like cake atop. It’s a marvel to watch as it bakes, and always a crowd pleaser. The recipe scores bonus points as an easy-peasy dessert to fill the bill for newer bakers to prepare for Mother’s Day. This recipe likely dates back to the late- ‘70’s from a fine food shop in Philadelphia. Since then, countless recipes have appeared, and I’ve tweaked my own version over the years. This one has less sugar but still retains a very deep, rich chocolate-y indulgence using a handful of few ingredients, many of which you likely have on hand most of the time! Take note: this cake has a unique process. The pudding layer is achieved by adding the ingredients in a very unconventional way. The thick cake batter forms the base, but then you add the “pudding” on top, which consists of brown sugar, more cocoa powder and hot coffee or water. The liquid=y pudding ingredients begin sinking once in the oven, and the resulting cake is atop the fudge-y pudding. It’s chemistry, or magic. You decide. • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted then cooled slightly 3/4 cup chocolate chips For the pudding: • 2/3 cup light brown sugar • 1/4 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 1-1/2 cups brewed coffee or very hot water INSTRUCTIONS Chocolate Pudding Cake Adapted from King Arthur Baking INGREDIENTS For the cake: • 1-1/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa, processed with alkali (“Dutch” process) • 3/4 cup whole milk, room temperature • 1 large egg, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Set a rimmed baking sheet on the rack to catch any drips and/or bake individual ramekins. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Butter an 8ʺ square pan, or eight 8-ounce ramekins. For the cake: In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and cocoa powder. Make sure there are no large clumps of cocoa powder, which you can pinch between your fingers to separate. Stir in the milk, egg, vanilla, and melted butter, mixing until smooth. Stir in the chocolate chips. Pour the batter into the prepared 8ʺ pan and spread evenly. If using eight ramekins portion a heaping 1/4-cup of batter into each. For the pudding: Mix the brown sugar with the cocoa powder in a small bowl then sprinkle this mixture evenly over the batter in the pan (or ramekins). Gently drizzle the hot coffer or water over the mixture. It is OK to fill the pan/ramekins pretty full as the cakes do not rise much. Bake for 45 minutes for an 8ʺ pan, or about 30 minutes for ramekins. Remove the cake when it looks set, and the pudding is bubbling around the edges of the pan. Remove from the oven and let cool for 15 minutes before serving. The pudding will thicken as it cools and is ideally served warm with ice cream. Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Some “did-you-knows” about estate plans If you’ve done any estate planning, or even if you’re just familiar with it, you probably know the basics — that is, a comprehensive estate plan can help you pass on assets to your family while also achieving other goals, such as designating someone to take care of your affairs if you become unable to do so. But you may not know about some other estate-planning issues that could prove important in your life: • Power of attorney for students Children heading off to college may be considered legal adults in many states. Consequently, you, as a parent, may not have any control over medical treatment if your child faces a sudden, serious illness or is involved in an accident. Instead, a doctor who doesn’t know your child or your family may decide on a course of action of which you might not approve. To help prevent this, you may want to have your college student sign a medical power of attorney form, which will allow you to make decisions on your child’s behalf if doctors don’t think your child can make those choices. You might also want to combine the medical power of attorney with an advance health care directive or living will, which lets you specify actions you do or don’t want to happen. In any case, consult with your legal advisor before taking any of these steps. • Community property versus common law Not all states treat married couples’ possessions equally. If you live in a community property state, the property you acquire during your marriage is generally considered to be owned in equal halves by each spouse, with some exceptions. But if you live in a common law state, the property you obtain while you’re married is not automatically owned by both spouses. In these states, if you buy some property, you own it, unless you decide to put it in the name of yourself and your spouse. This doesn’t necessarily mean that your spouse has no rights, because common law states typically have rules that guard surviving spouses from being disinherited. But here’s the key point: If you move from a community property state to a common law state, or vice versa, you might not want to assume that your and your spouse’s property ownership situations will remain the same. Consequently, if you do move, you may want to consult an estate-planning attorney in your new state to determine where you stand. • Pet trusts You always strive to take good care of your pets. But what might happen to them if you become incapacitated in some way? Unless you have a close family member or friend who’s willing to take over care for your pet, you might want to consider setting up a pet trust, which can take effect either during your lifetime or after you pass away. A trustee typically will make payments to the caregiver you’ve designated for your pet, with payments continuing for the pet’s lifetime or a set number of years. Again, an estate-planning attorney can help you with this arrangement. Estate planning certainly involves the big-picture issue of leaving a legacy to the next generation. But the issues we’ve discussed can also be meaningful to you, so you’ll want to address them properly. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Tickets are on sale now. General entry includes dinner, dessert, one beverage, as well as a full stage show with Taiko drummers, Bhangra, Flamenco, a Cuban salsa band and even an opera performance. Guests will be invited to explore the theme of “cultivating home” through physical mini marts constructed in the museum’s gardens. There will also be an area for kids’ activities with a continuous game of “found object soccer”, a basmati rice bag race, an immersive collaborative art piece and a silent auction of premier prizes. Craft cocktails, mocktails, wine, and beer will also be available, and additional food and drink will be available for purchase. He has written two books about the cemetery as well as books about Alameda and Oakland’s Laurel District. The walkers were told about the cemetery’s history, including his “three girlfriends” at the main mausoleum. They are statues of three women in its façade, and represent life, and how long it is measured. Dennis has a special interest in the renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863. He also planned New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. The cemetery is home to renowned 19th and 20th century individuals Charles Crocker, one of the founders of the Central Pacific Railroad, and architect Julia Morgan, among many. After the initial historical background, the group was led to a fountain on the cemetery’s main road.
